children.value: For the introductory level, you will be developing foundational skills in neuroscience research. Based on our guided exercise, you will write a research commentary of 500-1000 words summarizing your analyses, observations, and interpretations.
Writing a scientific report may feel unfamiliar if this is your first research project. Fortunately, many of the skills used by professional researchers can be learned through practice and guidance.

of both competition tracks, your written report will take the form of a research manuscript. We encourage you to communicate your research in a format similar to that used by scientists when sharing their work with the broader research community in a peer-reviewed journal.

For the competition, your written report will include an introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion, and abstract, and title.

There are no strict formatting requirements for written reports submitted to Connectome2026.
Participants are welcome to use any formatting style, provided that the report is
clear, readable, well-organized, and consistent throughout
That said, if you are unsure where to begin, the following conventions are commonly used in academic writing:
Font: Times New Roman, Arial, or Calibri.
Page margins: approximately 1 inch (2.54 cm) on all sides
Page numbering: recommended for longer reports
Section headings: clearly labelled and used consistently

Ultimately, judges will evaluate the content of your work rather than the specific formatting choices you make. However, it is important that you communicate your ideas and findings clearly and professionally.
For Advanced-Level submissions, we additionally recommend including clear section headings such as:
Declaration of Generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the writing process
The section order above follows a conventional manuscript structure:
Abstract → Introduction → Materials and Methods → Results → Discussion
However, you may notice that many published neuroscience papers use a different format:
Abstract → Introduction → Results → Discussion → Materials and Methods

at the end of the manuscript is common in many scientific journals, particularly in neuroscience and the life sciences. This allows readers to focus on the motivation and findings first, while the methodological details are presented later.
You are welcome to adopt either structure for your report. If this is your first research manuscript, however, we
. Regardless of the order you choose, ensure that all methodological details are described clearly enough for another researcher to reproduce your analysis.

You are required to have “Declaration of Generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the writing process” section heading in your report, even if you have not used generative AI. Note that participants will not be penalized for the responsible and transparent use of generative AI tools.
Please make sure to appropriately acknowledge any research papers, datasets, software tools (e.g.,

), figures, images, or other resources that you use in your report. Giving credit to the work of others is an important part of scientific research and allows readers to trace the sources of information, ideas, and methods used in your project.
If you are unfamiliar with academic referencing, we recommend reviewing the following guide:
Newcastle University Academic Skills Kit: Referencing
In brief, referencing means acknowledging the sources of information that you have used in your work.
This is generally a two-step process:
When referring to information, ideas, methods, datasets, or findings from another source, include a citation within the text of your report.
brain connectome was recently reconstructed using electron microscopy data (Scheffer et al., 2020).

is an in-text citation. It identifies the authors and publication year of the source from which the information originated. You insert the citation within the sentence to indicate the source of the information. In this case, the citation refers to the study by Scheffer and colleagues in 2020 (
), and it is formatted in APA style as (Scheffer et al., 2020).
There are many citation styles, including
. You are welcome to use any citation style, provided that you remain consistent throughout your report.
At the end of your report, include a
section containing the full bibliographic information for every source cited in the text. For example, the full APA-style reference would be:

Scheffer, L. K., Xu, C. S., Januszewski, M., Lu, Z., Takemura, S. Y., Hayworth, K. J., Huang, G. B., Shinomiya, K., Maitin-Shepard, J., Berg, S., Clements, J., Hubbard, P., Katz, W. T., Umayam, L. A., Zhao, T., Ackerman, D., Blakely, T., Bogovic, J., Dolafi, T., ... Plaza, S. M. (2020). A connectome and analysis of the adult
As a general rule, you should provide references for:
Software tools and platforms (e.g., Neuroglancer, neuPrint)
Figures, images, and visualizations that you did not create yourself
Methods, concepts, or ideas that originate from another source
When in doubt, it is usually better to provide a citation than to omit one.
Proper referencing is a fundamental part of scientific integrity and helps ensure that credit is given to the researchers and communities whose work supports your own.

neuPrint has become a widely used platform for exploring connectomics datasets (Plaza et al., 2022). Similarly, Neuroglancer provides an interactive environment for visualizing large-scale volumetric neuroscience data (Maitin-Shepard, 2020).
We recognize that there are multiple ways to cite software tools. The examples above are provided as recommended citations for participants who use neuPrint or Neuroglancer in their projects.
